\subsection{The CoT-Faith benchmark}
\label{app:sec:benchmark}
% ============================================================

CoT-Faith is designed around four selection principles: (P-1) \emph{faithfulness-specific:} each metric operationalizes CoT $\to$ action causal flow rather than surface task success; (P-2) \emph{null-controlled:} every metric has a validated null intervention with expected $\Delta\!=\!0$; (P-3) \emph{ablation-friendly:} models sharing base and data must be comparable, so training-target ablations are supported; (P-4) \emph{reproducible:} all edits, models, and metrics are code-released with a single-command reproduction of every reported cell.

\subsubsection{Task suite and prompt template}

We evaluate primarily on the Embodied-CoT LIBERO-90 dataset \citep{ecotlite}, which contains dense reasoning annotations across 90 LIBERO tasks spanning the four LIBERO suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, 10/Long). Each sample is a triple $(\text{img}, \text{instr}, \text{cot})$. The assistant turn follows the standard nine-tag ECoT template of \citet{ecot}:
\begin{center}\small
\texttt{USER: What action should the robot take to \{\allowbreak{}instr\}? ASSISTANT: TASK: \{\allowbreak{}...\} PLAN: \{\allowbreak{}...\} $\ldots$ GRIPPER POSITION: \{\allowbreak{}...\} ACTION: \{\allowbreak{}7 tokens\}}
\end{center}
Non-CoT baselines use the OpenVLA template, leaving the CoT segment empty. For the Bridge~V2 self-generated-CoT check (Section~\ref{sec:cross_corpus}) we use the raw Bridge~V2 lerobot-format dataset and let \texttt{ECoT-bridge} \emph{self-generate} its CoT via greedy decode; the same edit protocol is then applied to the model's own reasoning.

\subsubsection{Edit taxonomy (three semantic tiers, ten families, three calibration nulls)}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

CoT-Faith organizes edits by \emph{semantic depth} of the intervention:

\paragraph{Tier 0: surface / control ($\times 3$).} Interventions that should have zero or maximal effect if the metric is well-behaved.
\emph{selfsplice\_control:} identity substitution (X$\to$X). \emph{syntactic\_scramble:} word-order shuffle within \texttt{MOVE} and \texttt{SUBTASK}, preserving content words, and an LLM judge confirms it preserves \emph{meaning} at a rate of $1.000$ (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}), so it is best read as a second meaning-preserving family rather than as a structural edit. \emph{cross\_task\_swap:} replace the entire CoT with the reasoning from an unrelated LIBERO sample.

\paragraph{Tier 1: word-level semantic ($\times 4$).} Single-token or short-phrase swaps that mutate one semantic axis at a time. \emph{direction\_flip:} left$\leftrightarrow$right, up$\leftrightarrow$down, in$\leftrightarrow$out within \texttt{MOVE}. \emph{gripper\_flip:} grasp$\leftrightarrow$release, open$\leftrightarrow$close within \texttt{PLAN}/\texttt{SUBTASK}. \emph{verb\_swap:} action verbs $\to$ unrelated verbs, though an LLM judge finds the swap preserves meaning on $0.575$ of pairs (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}) rather than changing it, so this family is weaker than its name suggests. \emph{negation:} prepend ``do not'' to \texttt{SUBTASK}/\texttt{MOVE}.

\paragraph{Tier 2: object / causal-chain ($\times 3$).} Higher-order edits requiring cross-tag consistency. \emph{subject\_swap:} primary object referent $\to$ visible distractor across all reasoning tags. \emph{location\_swap:} spatial adverbs and 2-word location phrases within \texttt{PLAN}/\texttt{SUBTASK}/\texttt{TASK} (left/right, top/bottom, front/back, near/far, inside/outside, `left compartment' etc.). \emph{adversarial\_plausible:} object $\to$ second-most visible object, \emph{intended} to be visually plausible but wrong. An LLM judge confirms the referent changes ($0.958$) but rejects the plausibility half of that description: only $0.125$ of its edits are judged plausible (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}). We keep the family and the name, and readers should treat it as an unconstrained object substitution rather than as an adversarially plausible one.

\paragraph{Tier N: calibration nulls ($\times 3$).} Meaning-preserving perturbations whose score defines each model's \emph{floor}. Every reported $\mathcal{F}$ must be read against them, and we treat them as first-class families rather than sanity checks. \emph{paraphrase\_null:} synonym substitution within \texttt{MOVE}/\texttt{SUBTASK} that preserves the instruction's meaning. \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null:} $\pm 1$\,px perturbation of the \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS} bounding-box coordinates, below the resolution the reasoning operates at. \emph{instr\_random\_sub:} 5-token random substitution in the \emph{instruction} rather than the CoT, which measures each model's global prompt sensitivity from \emph{outside} the CoT segment and so bounds how much of any CoT-edit score is CoT-specific at all. (\emph{selfsplice\_control} above is the fourth, degenerate null: exact identity, expected and observed $0.00$.)

In total, $\mathbf{10}$ edit families across three semantic tiers (of which \emph{selfsplice\_control} is a degenerate identity null in behavior, though it is one of the $10$ rather than one of the $3$ calibration nulls below, leaving $9$ that carry a genuine semantic or structural edit), plus $\mathbf{3}$ calibration nulls: $\mathbf{13}$ families in all. Applied to $N{=}58$--$100$ LIBERO samples per model, with \emph{location\_swap} at $N\!\approx\!58$--$74$ after the annotation fix. Coverage: the calibration nulls have now been run on all $\mathbf{11}$ models in the benchmark, in both architecture families (the seven ``ours'' leaderboard rows at 3 sampling seeds each, ECoT-bridge, an independent retraining of the no-CoT variant, and the three DeepThinkVLA checkpoints), so every $\mathcal{F}$ in Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} has a measured floor and a measured ceiling from its own run, and the out-of-CoT specificity check is defined on every model (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}). One family is \emph{inapplicable} rather than unmeasured: \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null} perturbs bounding-box coordinates, and DeepThinkVLA's CoT renderer emits no bounding boxes, so the edit yields a byte-identical trace. The harness refuses to score an edit that does not survive rendering and records $n{=}0$ with all $100$ samples skipped, rather than returning the $\mathcal{F}=0.000$ that an unguarded run would report, a number that is indistinguishable from \emph{selfsplice\_control} and would read as robustness where in fact no perturbation reached the model.

\paragraph{Which capability each family probes, read as axes rather than as a flat list.} The thirteen families above are not thirteen unrelated perturbations; each targets one of six axes a CoT-conditioned policy's control could depend on, and a model's row in Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard}/Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard2} is a profile over these axes, not a single number: \emph{directional grounding} (\emph{direction\_flip}, \emph{gripper\_flip}: left/right, up/down, in/out, grasp/release); \emph{object and referent grounding} (\emph{subject\_swap}, \emph{adversarial\_plausible}: which visible object the reasoning names); \emph{spatial relation} (\emph{location\_swap}: which named place the action targets); \emph{action semantics} (\emph{verb\_swap}, \emph{negation}: which verb, and whether it is negated); \emph{full-CoT dependence} (\emph{cross\_task\_swap}: an entire unrelated reasoning trace); and \emph{instruction-vs-CoT attribution} (\emph{instr\_random\_sub}: whether a response comes from the instruction rather than the CoT segment at all). The four calibration families (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}) are not a seventh capability axis; they are the null every one of the six is read against. This grouping is descriptive of the existing edit families, not a new experiment, and we report it so that a future comparison can say a model is strong on one axis and weak on another rather than citing a single $\mathcal{F}$.

\subsubsection{Evaluation protocol, as a six-stage admission sequence}
\label{sec:eval_protocol}
The per-family calibration nulls, the selectivity test, the directional diagnostic, the collision check and the retraining bar are each introduced separately in the main text as the argument needs them; collected in one place, they are a single admission sequence a new model or a new edit family can be run through, restated here rather than newly designed.

\emph{Stage 1 -- Null calibration.} Score the model on all four null families (\emph{selfsplice\_control}, \emph{paraphrase\_null}, \emph{syntactic\_scramble}, \emph{instr\_random\_sub}; \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null} where the CoT renders bounding boxes). No stage below is interpretable without this one: \S\ref{sec:floors} is the paper-length version of what happens when it is skipped.

\emph{Stage 2 -- Selectivity.} Require $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{sem}}$ (the mean over the seven non-control semantic families) to exceed \emph{both} the paraphrase and the length-exact scramble null, per Eq.~\ref{eq:faith} at $\tau{=}0.05$ (\S\ref{sec:floors}). This is the test every model in this release fails: $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}} < 0$ against the paraphrase floor on $11$ of $11$ calibrated configurations (Table~\ref{tab:floors}).

\emph{Stage 3 -- Directional consistency.} For families with a signed semantic (\emph{direction\_flip}, \emph{gripper\_flip}, \emph{negation}), require $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:fdir}, $\cos < -0.5$) to clear the model's own null ceiling (\S\ref{sec:directional}). $7$ of $11$ configurations clear it here.

\emph{Stage 4 -- Decoder diagnostic.} Report the action-space collapse diagnostic (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix}) and, where feasible, the threshold-free $\overline{\text{TV}}$ (\S\ref{sec:collision}) beside every score in Stages 2--3, since both can inflate or deflate a magnitude score independent of semantic dependence.

\emph{Stage 5 -- Stability.} Require $|\Delta \mathcal{F}|$ between two same-recipe retraining replicates to be smaller than the model-to-model gap being reported (\S\ref{sec:variance}); $0.068$ is this release's own measured reference for the seven \texttt{Ours} configurations, not a universal constant for a model retrained on a different recipe.

\emph{Stage 6 -- Rollout validation (not run in this release).} Confirm that the step-level intervention effect in Stages 2--3 predicts closed-loop behavioural divergence under the same edit. This release does not clear this stage for any model, first-step-conditioned as it is throughout (\S\ref{sec:release}); it is left as the explicit next stage of the protocol rather than silently omitted.

A model or a new edit family is \emph{admissible} for a comparative claim only once it clears Stages 1--3 with Stage 4 reported alongside and Stage 5 satisfied; none of our own eight submissions clears Stage 2, so none is admissible by this protocol, which is the paper's own headline restated as a procedure.

\subsubsection{Evaluation protocol}
\label{sec:protocol_sampling}
\emph{Sample selection.} 100 first-step samples per condition; where compute permits, 3 file-shuffle seeds. \emph{Statistical protocol.} We report mean $\pm$ std across seeds where $\geq 2$ seeds exist, which is now every row of Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} (all 8 CoT-VLA rows at 3 seeds), and single-run point estimates with Wilson 95\% CIs otherwise (the three DeepThinkVLA runs); Wilson intervals on the 3-seed rows are computed on counts pooled over seeds. \emph{Reproducibility.} A single top-level script reproduces every reported cell in $\sim$3h on 8$\times$A100, and our audit script re-derives each number quoted in this paper from the released JSON and exits non-zero on any mismatch.

\subsection{Model scores, and why we do not publish them as a ranking}
\label{sec:results}
% ============================================================

Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} reports the magnitude score $\mathcal{F}(m, f)$ for every model$\times$family cell we measured: rows are the 8 CoT-VLA models (non-CoT baselines have no CoT to edit and are not part of this table), columns are the 10 non-null edit families plus one paraphrase-null (\emph{para}) organized by tier. Every row is a 3-seed mean$\pm$std of a single 13-family run of that checkpoint, so every cell in the table carries an error bar and the \emph{para} floor is populated on all 8 rows.

This table is a diagnostic, not a leaderboard, and the distinction is the paper's main methodological point. A per-model paraphrase floor is a \emph{required} field for admission to the public leaderboard. All 8 rows below carry one, and it disqualifies them rather than admitting them: on \emph{every} row the mean over the seven non-control families falls below that row's own floor ($\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}}$ from $-0.028$ to $-0.179$), so by our own admission rule none of our eight submissions is admissible, and the highest-scoring row (ECoT-bridge, the only public checkpoint among these eight) has a floor of $0.947$ at the same height as its maximum-effect ceiling of $0.963$, so its cells are not semantic sensitivity either. No subset licenses a ranking and we publish none: no cell is bolded and the row order is the configuration order of Table~\ref{tab:models}, not a score order. What the table is \emph{for} is the two structural findings it makes visible: that magnitude scores can sit on an unmeasured high floor (\S\ref{sec:floors}) and that they are direction-blind (Section~\ref{sec:directional}, final column). Take a comparative claim from $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ or $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$, never from the magnitude cells. Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} (main text) draws these same cells, plus Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard2}'s, as one surface.

\subsubsection{Self-generated CoT on Bridge~V2, the corpus \texttt{ECoT-bridge} is actually trained on}
\label{sec:cross_corpus}

Every result above teacher-forces or self-generates CoT on LIBERO, a corpus \texttt{ECoT-bridge} was not trained on. A follow-up run closes that gap for Bridge~V2 specifically: WidowX bimanual home manipulation, $N{=}100$, CoT self-generated via greedy decode since Bridge~V2 carries no ground-truth CoT annotations. Adding both calibration-null families to the self-decoded sample gives a paraphrase floor of $0.909$ ($n{=}99$) and a scramble floor of $0.802$ ($n{=}86$), against a semantic mean of $0.858$ over \emph{direction\_flip}/\emph{gripper\_flip} (\emph{subject\_swap} again admits $0$). The paraphrase floor sits \emph{above} the semantic mean, and the two floors disagree with each other ($0.107$) by more than either disagrees with the semantic mean ($0.051$/$0.056$): the same pattern \S\ref{sec:floors} reports on LIBERO with teacher-forced CoT, replicated in distribution, on self-generated CoT, on the one corpus this checkpoint was actually trained on.

\paragraph{A third floor, and it lies outside the CoT, in full.} \emph{instr\_random\_sub} corrupts five \emph{instruction} tokens and never touches the reasoning, so it bounds how much of any edit score is CoT$\to$action routing rather than generic prompt sensitivity. The specificity ratio $\bar{\mathcal{F}}/\mathcal{F}(\emph{instr\_random\_sub})$ exceeds $1$ on $5$ of the 11 configurations, so on those the semantic families do move the action more reliably than a corrupted instruction, but the margins ($+0.082$, $+0.074$, $+0.025$, $+0.014$ and $+0.009$ in $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$) are smaller than what retraining the same recipe moves the same statistic by, a median $0.044$ and up to $0.106$ across our six same-config pairs: no configuration in this benchmark clears its own out-of-CoT control by a margin that is clearly larger than its own retraining noise. The public checkpoint is below the control ($0.878$) and so is the entire second architecture family ($0.996$, $0.806$, $0.814$). We report this control on every row for that reason, and would require it of any submission.

\paragraph{The faithfulness threshold $\tau$, swept in full.} Both floor comparisons weaken with $\tau$: sweeping $\tau \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30\}$ over both floors, the paraphrase-floor sign count is $11$ negative at $\tau \le 0.10$, falls to $8$/$3$ at $\tau{=}0.20$, and to $6$/$5$, a near coin flip, at $\tau{=}0.30$, while the scramble-floor count stays stable ($10$--$9$ positive throughout). The paraphrase-floor claim is $\tau$-robust only up to $\tau{\approx}0.10$, roughly twice the reported threshold, a property of $\mathcal{F}$ specifically and not of the underlying effect: $\mathcal{F}$ has a $\tau$ to be robust \emph{to} only because it thresholds a continuous quantity, and \S\ref{sec:collision}'s threshold-free $\overline{\text{TV}}$ answers the same question with no $\tau$ to sweep, confirming the same floor collapse on every configuration it was run on.

\emph{A fixed $\tau{=}0.05$ is not the same physical threshold across architecture families.} DeepThinkVLA de-quantizes to each checkpoint's own LIBERO action quantiles (\texttt{q01}/\texttt{q99}) rather than the fixed $[-1,1]$ range the ECoT/LoRA rows use, and every one of its seven per-DoF physical widths is narrower than that range's $2.0$: $\tau{=}0.05$ is therefore $1.0$--$1.22\times$ stricter on the translation and gripper dimensions and $3.6$--$8.1\times$ stricter on the rotation dimensions for DeepThinkVLA, never more lenient. This does not invalidate any within-family comparison, and the bias runs against, not for, this table's below-floor finding on the DeepThinkVLA rows; but a cross-architecture aggregate (e.g.\ \S\ref{sec:floors}'s pooled ``9 of 11'') is comparing one normalized threshold applied at different physical strictness per family, verified here against the released \texttt{action\_decode} quantiles rather than assumed.


\subsubsection{Per-task decomposition: the below-floor result is not an artefact of averaging}
\label{sec:per_task}

Every $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ here averages over samples drawn from LIBERO-90 episodes, and an average can hide its shape in two ways a reviewer is entitled to ask about: the below-floor result could come from a minority of tasks on which the paraphrase edit happens to move the action a lot, leaving the majority above their floor; or $\mathcal{F}$ could be so task-dependent that a per-model number is not a property of the model at all. Neither question needs new inference, because every released edit record carries \texttt{file\_base}, the LIBERO episode file the observation came from, so $\mathcal{F}$ can be recomputed \emph{within} each task from the artifacts on disk.

\paragraph{Protocol, and the check that licenses the regrouping.} Pooling the three sampling seeds of each 3-seed run gives $\mathbf{85}$ distinct LIBERO-90 episode files, and it is the \emph{same} $85$ for all eight models, because every run draws from the same sampler seeds, so the test is paired across tasks and the columns are mutually comparable. Within each task we compute $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sem}}$, the macro average over the $7$ non-control families present for that task (at least $4$ of the $7$ on every task, from at least $5$ scored records), and that task's own $\mathcal{F}(\emph{paraphrase\_null})$, and report the \emph{sign} of the difference with an exact two-sided binomial test, ties dropped: a handful of samples makes each per-task floor coarse, but ``below its own floor on $k$ of $n$ tasks'' does not require the per-task means to be precise. Because a regrouping script can silently read a release differently from the pipeline that produced the leaderboard, it first re-derives each model's published $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ and paraphrase floor from the same records under the same convention and refuses to run if either disagrees by more than $10^{-9}$; all eight reproduce Table~\ref{tab:calibration} exactly.

\paragraph{Result: it holds task by task, on 7 of the 8 models.} Table~\ref{tab:per_task} gives the decomposition: on seven of the eight models the majority of tasks sit \emph{below} their own paraphrase floor, with two-sided $p$ from $9.0\!\times\!10^{-11}$ to $0.020$ and median per-task $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$ from $-0.167$ to $-0.050$, so the result is a property of most individual tasks and not of the average, which is what a per-model mean cannot establish on its own. The strongest cases are not the saturated one: \emph{r=32} is below on $64$ of $74$ untied tasks and \emph{r=8} on $60$ of $74$, against ECoT-bridge's $60$ of $75$. Restricting to the $53$ tasks whose floor rests on at least $3$ samples, so that no verdict comes from a single paraphrase draw, keeps six of the eight significant at $p<0.05$ and reverses no sign; \emph{data-50B} is the one row that loses significance ($0.020 \to 0.085$), and we report it as weakened rather than as surviving.

\paragraph{The one exception is the positive control, which we did not predict in advance.} \emph{Ours no-CoT} is the model whose per-task test is null ($25$ below, $29$ above, $31$ tied, $p = 0.683$), and it is the checkpoint trained on an action-only target, whose whole-run margin is the smallest in the benchmark at $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}} = -0.028$: a model sitting essentially \emph{on} its own floor in aggregate should scatter around it per task, and it does. The per-task test therefore agrees with the aggregate on which model is the exception, which is a coherence check rather than a counterexample, and we state it as post hoc.

\paragraph{The second question is answered less favourably: $\mathcal{F}$ is heavily task-dependent, and the leaderboard gaps do not clear it.} The within-model interquartile range of $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sem}}$ across tasks runs from $0.129$ (ECoT-bridge) to $0.343$ (\emph{r=16}), and on three of the eight models the task range is the entire unit interval: the same checkpoint scores $0.00$ on some LIBERO-90 tasks and $1.00$ on others. Ordering the eight models by $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$, 6 of the 7 adjacent gaps are smaller than both models' task-level IQR, the largest such gap being $0.187$; the only adjacent pair that separates at task granularity is \emph{r=64} versus ECoT-bridge at $0.346$. So with one exception, differences between rows of this leaderboard are smaller than the variation a single row already contains across the tasks it was measured on, which is independent support for the position Section~\ref{sec:results} takes for other reasons. It also bounds the decomposition: the sign test is a statement about a fixed set of $85$ tasks, and that spread is why we do not read the per-task medians as effect sizes.

\paragraph{What this decomposition cannot do.} It decomposes the \emph{edit} protocol only. A per-task breakdown of rollout success rate would answer a different question and is not derivable from the release: the four-suite gate artifacts store per-arm aggregates (\texttt{sr\_by\_arm} over $10$ tasks $\times$ $5$ episodes) and not per-task outcomes, so it needs new rollouts, which this submission does not have.

\subsubsection{Pseudo-replication, made explicit: how many independent confirmations is ``9 of 11'' actually}
\label{sec:pseudoreplication}

\S\ref{sec:floors} discloses that the eleven calibrated configurations are two base-checkpoint lineages, not eleven independent replications: eight rows are \texttt{ECoT-bridge} or a LoRA adapter on it, three are \texttt{DeepThinkVLA-base} stages. That disclosure does not by itself say what ``significant on 9 of 11'' is worth given that structure. Each configuration's own paired, observation-clustered bootstrap is a valid test of \emph{that} configuration (it correctly captures the uncertainty in which observations were drawn), but the eight ECoT-lineage configurations share a base checkpoint, a training corpus, and, for the seven \texttt{Ours} rows, the same $85$ LIBERO-90 episode files. Their results are not eight (or, with \texttt{ECoT-bridge}, nine) independent pieces of evidence for the headline; at best they are as many independent pieces of evidence as there are independent lineages, which is two.

A third, weaker but genuinely independent data point exists outside this release entirely: \citet{vladrivebench}'s own Table 13, re-read in \S\ref{sec:related}, shows the identical floor-collapse pattern (a meaning-destroying control moving their driving VLA's continuous output at least as much as a meaningful prompt) on a different model, a different modality (driving, not manipulation), and a different research group's own reported numbers, not ours. It does not raise the lineage count to three: it is secondhand (their ablation, not a rerun under our protocol), reported by its authors as a property of their specific prompts rather than generalized into a claim about the scoring rule, and we have not re-derived it under the calibrated-floor methodology \S\ref{sec:floors} uses here. What it does do is make ``this is a quirk of these two lineages'' a harder claim to sustain than the pooled configuration count alone would suggest.

Made explicit rather than left for a reader to reconstruct: within the ECoT lineage, $7$ of $8$ configurations are individually significant (every \texttt{Ours} LoRA variant and \texttt{ECoT-bridge}; \texttt{no-CoT} is the exception); within the DeepThinkVLA lineage, $2$ of $3$ are (\texttt{DT SFT} and \texttt{DT RL}; \texttt{DT base} is the exception). Pooled, that is the manuscript's $9$ of $11$. Reported by lineage, it is two independent confirmations of the same qualitative result (floor-collapse, significant in the majority of each lineage's own configurations), not nine, and the one exception in each lineage is the same \emph{kind} of exception: the row closest to its own floor, which is what a null control (\texttt{no-CoT}) and what turns out to behave like one (\texttt{DT base}, per \S\ref{sec:floors}) should both look like.

The two confirmations are not equally precise, either. The ECoT lineage's significance rests on 3 sampling seeds per configuration (Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard}); the DeepThinkVLA lineage's rests on one seed per checkpoint ($^\dagger$ throughout, e.g.\ Table~\ref{tab:calibration}), so its Wilson intervals bound the sample draw only and run-to-run training variance (the error bar \S\ref{sec:variance} shows matters more than sampling for the ECoT lineage) is not measured for DeepThinkVLA at all. ``2 of 3'' is therefore the finer-grained honest count, not a confirmation of comparable statistical power to the ECoT lineage's ``7 of 8''.

We do not fit a hierarchical or cluster-robust model with lineage as a random effect, and say so rather than paper over it: such a model needs enough clusters to estimate a between-cluster variance component, and two clusters supply two data points for that estimate, which is not enough to fit anything rather than merely narrate one. A lineage-level $p$-value would manufacture a precision this design cannot support. What is reported above (the within-lineage sign and significance count) is the finest-grained statement the data honestly permit, and it is what \S\ref{sec:floors}'s parenthetical now states directly rather than leaving to be reconstructed from the per-config table.

\subsubsection{Multiplicity correction and bootstrap methodology, made explicit}
\label{sec:multiplicity}

Table~\ref{tab:floors}'s ``9 of 11''/``3 of 11'' and Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}'s ``6 of 6''/``5 of 6'' are each a family of paired, observation-clustered bootstraps ($B{=}20{,}000$ resamples, percentile $95\%$ interval): $11$ configurations $\times$ 2 floors for the first, $6\times 2$ for the second, none corrected for running that many tests at once except where \S\ref{sec:variance}'s Multiplicity paragraph already states the one exception (the $8$ per-task tests). Two questions follow from that, both checked here rather than asserted: does a plain percentile interval understate uncertainty relative to a bias-and-skewness-corrected one, given that the underlying statistic ($\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}}$ or $\overline{\text{TV}}_{\text{diff}}$) can sit near a $[-1,1]$ boundary; and what survives once each table's family-wise error rate is controlled, rather than reading every configuration's own $95\%$ interval as if it were the only test run.

Bootstrap method, re-derived with a bias-and-acceleration correction: it does not change a single verdict. For all $34$ tests ($11\!\times\!2$ plus $6\!\times\!2$) we recomputed the identical resampling (same seed, same $B{=}20{,}000$, same paired observation clusters as \S\ref{sec:variance} and \S\ref{sec:collision}) and checked the recomputed percentile interval's significance verdict against the manuscript's stored one before trusting anything built on top of it; it matches on all $34$. We then derived a BCa interval for each: bias $z_0 = \Phi^{-1}\!\bigl(\hat P(\theta^{*}<\hat\theta)\bigr)$ from the bootstrap draws themselves, acceleration $\hat a$ from a leave-one-observation-out jackknife of the same statistic, and BCa-adjusted percentiles (via $\Phi$, inverted by bisection rather than a rational approximation) in place of the fixed $2.5$/$97.5$ ones. The BCa verdict matches the plain-percentile verdict on all $34$ tests: $9$/$11$ and $3$/$11$ (Table~\ref{tab:floors}), $6$/$6$ and $5$/$6$ (Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}), unchanged either way. The boundary-proximity concern motivating BCa does not materialize in this data.

Bootstrap resampling unit, re-derived at the LIBERO episode-file level: it does not change a single verdict either. Table~\ref{tab:floors}'s $22$ tests resample $(\text{seed}, \text{sample})$ pairs, which \S\ref{sec:per_task} independently shows are not exchangeable: within-model task-level $\mathcal{F}_{\text{sem}}$ IQR runs up to $0.343$, so two observations from the same LIBERO-90 episode file are more alike than two from different files, and treating each sample as its own resampling unit when several samples per configuration share a file could understate uncertainty. It does not, here: re-clustering every one of the $22$ tests at the file level ($61$--$85$ distinct files per configuration, up to $4$ samples sharing one file) rather than the sample level, using the same statistic (\texttt{scripts/\allowbreak{}bootstrap\_multiplicity\_bca.py}'s \texttt{binary\_diff\_stat}, imported rather than reimplemented so the two designs cannot silently diverge), the same $\tau$, and the same $B{=}20{,}000$, reproduces the identical significance verdict on all $22$ tests, configuration by configuration: $9$/$11$ paraphrase, $3$/$11$ scramble, and the exact same nine and three rows, not merely the same counts (\texttt{results\_v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_runs/\allowbreak{}floor\_bootstrap\_file\_clustered/}). The per-task decomposition's own within-file correlation is real (it is why \S\ref{sec:per_task} exists) but it is not large enough, relative to the between-condition gap each of these $22$ tests measures, to move any of them across the significance boundary.

\emph{The three bins spanning $\tau$, and why the metric is insensitive to it.} The bins are unequal-width ($0.005$/$0.045$/$0.05$), and in density (count per unit width) terms the bin immediately below $\tau$ is the densest of the three, not a valley: it is the $90.7\%$ combined share on either side of $\tau$ (\S\ref{sec:collision}), not a density gap at $\tau$ specifically, that makes $\mathcal{F}$ insensitive to where the threshold sits. The relation between $\mathcal{F}$ and $1{-}P(\Delta_\infty{=}0)$ (\S\ref{sec:collision}) is one-sided, not a two-sided identity: of the 324 (run, family) cells, $0$ lie above the drawn $y{=}x$ line, $244$ lie below it, and $80$ sit exactly on it, since $\{\Delta_\infty{>}\tau\} \subseteq \{\Delta_\infty{\neq}0\}$ by construction.

The two $R^2$ values in \S\ref{sec:collision}, and which convention each uses, stated explicitly. $R^2{=}0.926$ is the best-fit-line correlation between $\mathcal{F}$ and $1{-}P(\Delta_\infty{=}0)$. $R^2{=}0.893$ anchors instead on the drawn $y{=}x$ line itself, with $\mathcal{F}$ as the response and $1{-}P(\Delta_\infty{=}0)$ as the reference prediction: $\text{SS}_{\text{tot}}$ from $\mathcal{F}$'s own variance around its mean, $\text{SS}_{\text{res}}$ from each cell's deviation off $y{=}x$. Anchoring $\text{SS}_{\text{tot}}$ on $1{-}P(\Delta_\infty{=}0)$'s variance instead (treating the collision indicator, not $\mathcal{F}$, as the response) gives $0.899$, a different but equally defensible convention; we report the one matching which quantity \S\ref{sec:collision} treats as the thing being explained (\texttt{scripts/\allowbreak{}verify\_paper\_numbers.py}'s \texttt{audit\_\allowbreak{}collision\_decomposition}, which computes this independently of \texttt{collision\_\allowbreak{}decomposition.json}'s own stored best-fit field).

Multiplicity, corrected within each table's own family of tests, the same Holm step-down \S\ref{sec:variance} already applies to the eight per-task tests. Table~\ref{tab:multiplicity} gives every count from a two-sided bootstrap $p$-value ($p = 2\min(\hat P(\theta^{*}{\le}0), \hat P(\theta^{*}{\ge}0))$, ceilinged at $1$) Holm-corrected at $\alpha{=}0.05$ across each table's tests. Correcting Table~\ref{tab:floors}'s $22$ tests lowers its counts to $7$/$11$ (paraphrase) and $1$/$11$ (scramble); correcting Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}'s $12$ lowers its counts to $2$/$6$ (paraphrase) and $5$/$6$ (scramble, unchanged). The scramble-floor counts were already reported as a small minority in the main text (``only 3 reversals are significant''); Holm correction does not change that qualitative reading. The paraphrase-floor counts are what move, and Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}'s is the largest single change in this section: ``all six significant'' becomes two of six once corrected for testing six configurations at once. What Holm correction does not touch is the sign pattern that \S\ref{sec:floors} actually turns on: $11$ of $11$ (Table~\ref{tab:floors}) and $6$ of $6$ (Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}) configurations have the paraphrase floor at or above the semantic mean, before any significance test is run on top of that comparison.

\subsubsection{Per-family heterogeneity: the below-floor result is not an artefact of averaging across families either}
\label{sec:family_heterogeneity}

$\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ averages over seven semantic families as well as over samples, and a reader who computes each family's own rate from the per-model tables (Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard}, Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard2}, Table~\ref{tab:calibration}) will find a sharp split, not a uniform below-floor pattern: across the eleven calibrated configurations, \emph{negation} clears the paraphrase floor on all eleven and \emph{direction\_flip} on nine, while \emph{gripper\_flip} and \emph{location\_swap} clear it on none and \emph{subject\_swap} on four. Read alone, that looks like it could put the whole below-floor result at the mercy of which families are included and how they are weighted: a family-level averaging artifact competing with \S\ref{sec:floors}'s claim rather than supporting it.

It does not, and the reason is the one \S\ref{sec:collision} already gives for a different pattern in the same data. We computed each family's own share of records where the policy's argmax action bin does not move at all ($1 - P(\Delta_\infty{=}0)$, from the same $324$ (run, family) cells \S\ref{sec:collision} correlates against $\mathcal{F}$ at $R^2{=}0.926$) and compared it against how often that family clears the paraphrase floor across the eleven configurations. The two track each other closely: Spearman $\rho = 0.883$ ($n{=}7$ families, average-rank tie-breaking, Fisher-$z$ 95\% CI $[0.388, 0.983]$; Table~\ref{tab:family_het}). \emph{negation} (clears $11$ of $11$, mean non-collision $0.689$) and \emph{direction\_flip} ($9$ of $11$, $0.746$) are exactly the families whose edits reliably flip the policy's argmax bin; \emph{gripper\_flip} ($0$ of $11$, $0.349$) and \emph{location\_swap} ($0$ of $11$, $0.328$) are exactly the families that rarely do. A family that mechanically produces a large action-space perturbation clears the floor regardless of how much meaning it changes, and a family that mechanically produces a small one does not clear it for the same mechanical reason, independent of meaning, which is \S\ref{sec:collision}'s diagnosis restated one level down, not a competing explanation for the family split. The heterogeneity a reviewer finds by hand computing per-family rates is evidence for the mechanism the paper already claims, not against the headline that mechanism supports.

\subsubsection{Do the edit families do what their names say? An LLM-judge validation of the generators}
\label{sec:judge_edits}

Every result in this paper is conditional on a set of claims we had asserted from generator source code and never measured: that \emph{paraphrase\_null} preserves meaning, that \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null} perturbs a number without touching semantics, that \emph{adversarial\_plausible} substitutes an object that stays visually plausible. These are not decorative. $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$ is a floor-corrected statistic \emph{only} if the floor family really is meaning-preserving, so the central negative result of \S\ref{sec:floors} ($\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ below the paraphrase floor on $11$ of $12$ calibrations) rests on a premise that had the same evidential status as the caveats this revision has been replacing with measurements. So we measured it.

\paragraph{Protocol.} An independent LLM judge (\texttt{Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct}, neither of the architecture families under test) reads each $(\text{original}, \text{edited})$ reasoning pair and answers four binary questions (meaning preserved, same referent, same direction, still plausible) plus a $1$--$5$ fluency rating. It is blind to which family produced the pair and never sees the model's action. $480$ pairs were constructed over $40$ samples $\times$ $11$ families plus an identity control; $437$ were judged and all $43$ skips are itemized, every one of them a case where the \emph{generator} found no applicable edit ($16$ \emph{adversarial\_plausible}, $16$ \emph{subject\_swap}, $10$ \emph{location\_swap}) plus one identical render.

\paragraph{The judge is itself gated, on three checks, before any of its rates are read.} A judge that answers ``preserved'' unconditionally would validate every null in the paper, so the identity check alone is not enough. (a) \emph{Identity control}: on $40$ pairs where the edit is $X \to X$, preserved rate $= \mathbf{1.000}$. (b) \emph{Negative control}: pooled over the families designed to destroy meaning, preserved rate $= \mathbf{0.175}$, which is what rules out the degenerate judge the first gate would pass. (c) \emph{Order agreement}: presenting the two traces in the opposite order changes the verdict on $77$ of $437$ pairs, so agreement is $\mathbf{0.824}$, a real presentation bias, and the noise floor to attach to every rate below. All three pass and the run is marked valid.

\paragraph{A second judge model was run on the same 437 pairs, and it fails this gate.} \texttt{Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2} \citep{mistral7b}, same protocol, same pairs: identity control $\mathbf{1.000}$ and order agreement $\mathbf{0.973}$ both pass, but the negative control (the gate that rules out a degenerate ``always preserved'' judge) comes back at $\mathbf{0.943}$ pooled preserved rate on the families designed to destroy meaning, against Qwen's $0.175$ on the identical pairs. This judge is invalid by its own gate, not merely noisier: it calls an edit meaning-preserving $94.3\%$ of the time even when the edit is designed not to be, which is close to the unconditional-``preserved'' judge the gate exists to catch. We report this rather than silently drop the run, and it is the reason \S\ref{sec:benchmark} says agreement between the two judges is not treated as independent corroboration: corroboration from an invalid judge is not corroboration, and this paper's floor-validation premise rests on the one judge that passes all three gates, not on a majority vote across two.

\paragraph{Three of four declared premises hold; the fourth fails.} \emph{paraphrase\_null} preserves meaning at $0.975$ (Wilson $95\%$ CI $[0.871, 0.996]$, $n{=}40$; fluency $4.92$) and \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null} at $1.000$ ($[0.912, 1.000]$, $n{=}40$; fluency $5.00$). The two nulls that $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$ and the numeric-floor argument depend on are validated, which is the outcome those arguments needed and did not previously have. \emph{syntactic\_scramble} also comes back at $1.000$ ($[0.912, 1.000]$). These intervals are wide at $n{=}40$ (paraphrase\_null's lower bound sits $10$\,pp below its point estimate), which is the honest cost of a single-judge, $n{=}40$-per-family design; \S\ref{sec:judge_edits}'s ``What this does not establish'' paragraph already flags reading these to two decimal places at most, and the interval width is why. But \emph{adversarial\_plausible} fails: the referent changes on $0.958$ of pairs, as designed, while only $\mathbf{0.125}$ of its edits are judged plausible against a taxonomy entry that called them ``visually plausible but wrong''. Counting the $16$ samples where the generator produced no edit at all, the family delivers a plausible substitution on $3$ of $40$ attempts. The ``second-most visible object'' heuristic does not produce plausible substitutions, so \emph{adversarial\_plausible} has been measuring an unconstrained object swap, which is a weaker intervention than its name claims and one that overlaps \emph{subject\_swap} more than we intended. We do not delete the family or its numbers: its $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$ ($-0.014$ on ECoT-bridge) are unaffected by what the edit is \emph{called}; we correct the description, in Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} and here. No claim in this paper turns on the plausibility of that family; had one done so, this measurement would have withdrawn it.

A fourth null, added later and validated separately (\S\ref{sec:floors}'s length-decoupling check): \emph{paraphrase\_null\_lenexact} preserves meaning at $1.000$ with fluency $4.92$, on its own $40$-pair run against a \emph{direction\_flip} negative control ($n_{\text{pairs}}{=}120$, $119$ judged, identity/negative/order gates all pass; the first attempt at this run used no negative control, failed its own validity gate by construction, and is not the run these numbers come from).

\paragraph{Two findings we were not looking for.} First, \emph{syntactic\_scramble} at a preserved rate of $1.000$ is a \emph{third} meaning-preserving family, and it is listed in Tier~0 as a structural edit. Its $\mathcal{F}$ is therefore a second within-CoT surface-form floor, independent of \emph{paraphrase\_null}'s lexical route to the same thing, which strengthens rather than weakens the below-floor result: two unrelated ways of preserving meaning both move the action. Second, \emph{verb\_swap} preserves meaning on $0.575$ of pairs (changes it on only $0.425$) and changes the implied direction on $0.650$, so roughly $6$ in $10$ ``verb swaps'' are not semantic edits at all. This is the same family that carries the largest same-config retraining movement in the benchmark ($\max|\Delta\mathcal{F}| = 0.317$ on $r{=}8$, worst family on $2$ of the $6$ retraining pairs, \S\ref{sec:variance}): the least semantically reliable generator is also the noisiest cell, and we now think those two facts are the same fact. The families with no declared premise behave as intended: \emph{cross\_task\_swap} preserves meaning on $0.025$, \emph{gripper\_flip} on $0.050$, \emph{negation} on $0.100$, and \emph{direction\_flip} on $0.200$ while holding the referent at $1.000$ and changing the direction on all $40$.

\paragraph{What this does not establish.} The judge validates the \emph{generators}, not the specific pairs that produced any published number. The released edit records store actions only, and demo/step identity is not recoverable without re-iterating the $17$\,GB tfds shards, so the judge re-runs the same generators over the same corpus, restricted to the demo files the scored run drew from. It is also one judge model at $n{=}40$ per family, with a measured $17.6\%$ order-flip rate, so these rates should be read to two decimal places at most. The released artifact carries the report and all $437$ judged pairs with both traces.

\subsubsection{A positive control: a rule-based oracle, so \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$}{F\_dir}=1 is a property of the construction, not a hope}
\label{sec:oracle}

Every $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ elsewhere in this paper is measured on a trained neural policy, so a low score is always compatible with an explanation this paper has not been arguing for: the instrument itself cannot detect faithfulness even when it is genuinely present. We rule this out with a ``policy'' that has no network in it at all. The oracle reads the MOVE phrase text and nothing else (no image, no instruction, no learned weights) and returns a fixed 7-DoF vector: each of the eight direction words \emph{direction\_flip} itself flips (the same word-pair table that edit family uses) is mapped by a hand-written table to $\pm 1$ on one of three translation axes (\texttt{left}/\texttt{right} $\to y$, \texttt{forward}/\texttt{back} $\to x$, \texttt{up}/\texttt{above}/\texttt{down}/\texttt{below} $\to z$), multiple words in one phrase compose, and the same string always returns the same vector. The rotation and gripper dimensions are fixed at $0$. This is not a claim about what a real policy does; it is a claim about what a MOVE-conditioned action generator, built to be one, does.

Applied to the released judge-validation pairs (\texttt{judge\_edit\_families/\allowbreak{}judge\_pairs.json}, the same $(a\_head, b\_head)$ text pairs \S\ref{sec:judge_edits} scores with an LLM judge, not a new capture), on the two families that bear on this directly: \emph{paraphrase\_null} ($N{=}40$) substitutes \texttt{move}$\to$\texttt{shift} and leaves every direction word untouched, verified on all 40 pairs before running anything; the oracle's action is therefore byte-identical on all 40, $\Delta_\infty = 0$ exactly, $\mathcal{F}_{\text{mag}} = \mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} = 0.000$. \emph{direction\_flip} ($N{=}40$) inverts them: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{mag}} = 1.000$ (every sample moves), $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} = 0.925$ (37 of 40 reverse, mean cosine $-0.925$). The three non-reversing samples are not noise; they are a named limit of this simple parser: each mixes a translation direction word with a same-named \emph{rotation} direction word in one phrase (e.g.\ ``move down and forward and left and \emph{rotate up}''), and a word-only parser that does not distinguish the two contexts lets the later match overwrite the earlier one on the shared $z$ axis. A parser that scoped words to their clause would likely recover all three; we did not build one, because $0.925$ against every real checkpoint's $\leq 0.117$ already makes the point, and patching the parser to reach exactly $1.000$ would cost more engineering than the extra $0.075$ is worth.

$\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} = 0.925$ against the highest real checkpoint's $0.117$ (\texttt{ECoT-bridge}, Table~\ref{tab:directional}) is an $8\times$ gap, not a subtle one, and $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}=0.000$ on \emph{paraphrase\_null} is the same floor-respecting behaviour \S\ref{sec:floors} asks of every real model. Both numbers are consequences of the construction, checkable by reading the oracle function, not measurements with sampling uncertainty attached to them; that is the point of an oracle sanity check, and it is why $n{=}40$ per family is enough here even though it would not be enough for a comparative claim between two real checkpoints elsewhere in this paper. The construction is deliberately narrow: it says the diagnostic can register a difference this large when one is really there, not that any real checkpoint's low score is explained by the same mechanism the oracle uses, and not that the oracle's own $\mathcal{F}_{\text{mag}}=1.000$ says anything about a family other than the two tested here.

\paragraph{A two-point oracle only tests one causal dependence against one absence of it; sweeping a mixing weight tests whether $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ tracks the \emph{degree} of CoT-dependence in between.} \texttt{experiments/\allowbreak{}cot\_mixed\_policy\_sweep.py} builds a family of synthetic policies on the same \emph{direction\_flip} pairs: $a(\alpha) = \alpha \cdot f(\text{CoT}_{\text{edited}}) + (1-\alpha) \cdot g(\text{CoT}_{\text{ignored}})$, where $f$ is the oracle above applied to the edited MOVE phrase and $g$ is the same oracle applied to the \emph{original} phrase, i.e.\ a policy that ignores the CoT edit exactly as if it were grounded in the unedited image or instruction instead. At $\alpha{=}1$ this is the oracle above ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}=0.925$); at $\alpha{=}0$ the ``edited'' action is byte-identical to the original on every sample, so $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}=0$ by construction, the same way \emph{paraphrase\_null} is. Sweeping $\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.1, \ldots, 1.0\}$: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}(\alpha)$ is $0.000$ for $\alpha \leq 0.4$ and $0.925$ for $\alpha \geq 0.6$, monotone non-decreasing across the full grid with no reversal, and mean cosine moves from $+1.000$ ($\alpha{=}0$) to $-0.925$ ($\alpha{=}1$) passing through $+0.987$ at $\alpha{=}0.4$ and $-0.885$ at $\alpha{=}0.6$. This is not a smooth ramp: because \emph{direction\_flip}'s two endpoints are (by construction) near-antipodal on the axes each MOVE phrase uses, linearly mixing them scales the vector down to (numerically) zero at $\alpha{=}0.5$ -- only $3$ of $40$ pairs have a defined cosine there, the same $3$ exceptions the oracle above already names -- and flips its sign on either side, so $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ steps rather than ramps. The sweep therefore confirms monotonicity, the property a diagnostic with construct validity should have as CoT-dependence increases, but on a two-point-mixture construction rather than a smoothly graded one; it does not by itself establish that $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ resolves finer degrees of partial CoT-dependence, which a policy family with continuously varying, non-antipodal mixing directions would be needed to test.

\subsection{Release and audit, in full}
\label{sec:release}

We release $52{,}338$ per-sample edit records ($45{,}989$ scored) as $77.4$\,MB of self-contained JSON, under a permissive licence (CC~BY~4.0; code separately under MIT; \texttt{LICENSE}); our audit script asserts 1,632 claims against these and every other released artifact and exits non-zero on any mismatch. $\Delta_\infty$ is not invalidated, but six of the eight leaderboard rows come from a policy whose single-step open-loop prediction does not beat a constant, which is why no number here is rollout-conditioned (\S\ref{sec:limitations_full}). Our admission rule requires a paraphrase floor and a direction check per model; it admits none of our eight submissions: all score below floor ($\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}}$ $-0.027$ to $-0.180$), best still $0.017$ under ceiling.

\subsection{Limitations, in full}
\label{sec:limitations_full}

The main text's Limitations gives the load-bearing items in one line each; this is the detail behind every one of them, in the same order.

\emph{The self-generated-CoT check is small and mixed, not a clean replication.} Every other number in this paper edits a teacher-forced ground-truth CoT annotation, not any model's own generated reasoning. Rerunning the floor comparison on CoT each checkpoint generates online (\texttt{ECoT-bridge}, \texttt{r=32}, \texttt{no-CoT}) replicates closely on \texttt{ECoT-bridge} ($\overline{\text{TV}}_{\text{diff}}$ vs.\ paraphrase $-0.072$, significant, matching Table~\ref{tab:tvfloors}'s teacher-forced value almost exactly) but \emph{reverses sign} on \texttt{r=32} ($+0.021$, significant), and is inconclusive on \texttt{no-CoT}. We read this as neither confirming nor refuting the teacher-forced result in general: it is evidence the floor collapse can depend on whether the CoT is teacher-forced or self-generated on at least one configuration, and three self-generated-CoT checkpoints from one architecture family are not enough to say which behaviour is typical. A fourth checkpoint in this lineage, \texttt{r=64} (run separately, $N{=}100$ plus a $40$-sample timestep addon), complicates rather than resolves this: on the same $\overline{\text{TV}}_{\text{diff}}$ statistic (mean over the five semantic families with any usable self-generated sample here; \emph{subject\_swap} and \emph{adversarial\_plausible} again score zero) the reversal is close to null ($+0.006$), but on \emph{direction\_flip} alone, pooling the base run and the addon, it is large and significant ($\overline{\text{TV}} = 0.371$ against $0.182$ for \emph{paraphrase\_null}, $+0.189$, bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[0.169, 0.208]$), the same family the memorization check below already isolates for teacher-forced \texttt{r=32}. Whether \texttt{r=64} ``reverses'' depends on which of these two statistics is read, itself a smaller-scale instance of \S\ref{sec:floors}'s point about which floor is read: four self-generated-CoT checkpoints from one architecture family, with a picture that changes even within a single checkpoint depending on the statistic, are not enough to say which behaviour is typical. Separately, four of our thirteen families (\emph{subject\_swap}, \emph{adversarial\_plausible}, \emph{selfsplice\_control}, \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null}) score zero usable samples on all self-generated checkpoints tested: their generators look for a substring (a subject noun phrase, an object mention, an exact self-splice match, a bounding-box literal) that self-generated CoT text essentially never contains verbatim, a limit of the generators rather than evidence about the models.

\emph{A fifth and sixth self-generated-CoT checkpoint, both from the second architecture family, replicate the floor collapse and the direction-reversal (\texttt{DT-RL}) or point the same direction without reaching significance at this $n$ (\texttt{DT-SFT}).} \texttt{DeepThinkVLA-RL} free-generates a well-formed CoT often enough to support this check at $n{=}1000$ samples (997 usable for \emph{paraphrase\_null}, 43 for \emph{direction\_flip} after the same generator-applicability gate as the teacher-forced runs). On self-generated CoT its \emph{paraphrase\_null} faithful rate ($0.363$) exceeds its \emph{direction\_flip} rate ($0.233$), the same floor-above-semantic pattern \S\ref{sec:floors} reports teacher-forced, paired on the $43$ shared samples and significant (bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[-0.419, -0.047]$). Its direction-aware score on this same self-generated cohort is $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}{=}0.000$ with mean translation cosine $+0.969$, i.e.\ \emph{more} extreme non-reversal than the teacher-forced row in Table~\ref{tab:directional} ($0.010$, $+0.915$), not less. \texttt{DeepThinkVLA-SFT}, the same architecture at its supervised-only training stage, gives the same comparison at the same $N{=}1000$ (997 usable for \emph{paraphrase\_null}, 41 for \emph{direction\_flip}): faithful rate $0.364$ against $0.268$, the same direction as \texttt{DT-RL}; but paired on the $41$ samples where both families have a usable record (\emph{paraphrase\_null} restricted to this smaller subset reads $0.463$, not $0.364$), the gap does not reach significance at this $n$ (bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[-0.390, 0.0]$, touching zero). Its direction-aware score on the same cohort is $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}{=}0.000$ with mean translation cosine $+0.960$ ($n{=}41$), matching \texttt{DT-RL}'s non-reversal in kind if not in statistical confidence. So both self-generated-CoT checkpoints we have outside the ECoT lineage move in the direction opposite to \texttt{r=32}'s reversal above: they point toward strengthening, not weakening, the teacher-forced finding for that lineage, though only one of the two clears significance on its own paired test. Six checkpoints across two lineages -- three replicating cleanly (\texttt{ECoT-bridge}, \texttt{DT-RL}, and directionally \texttt{DT-SFT}), one reversing cleanly (\texttt{r=32}), one mixed depending on which statistic is read (\texttt{r=64}), one inconclusive (\texttt{no-CoT}) -- is still a small, heterogeneous cohort, and we do not read it as closing this gap.

\emph{An admission rule, stated as a conjunction, in full.} Admit a model's score only if, per family: (i) $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}}$ against the paraphrase floor exceeds \S\ref{sec:variance}'s $0.068$ retraining bar in the faithful direction (a measured bound for the seven \texttt{Ours} configurations, a reference value elsewhere; \S\ref{sec:floors}), and, for every signed family, (ii) $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ clears its own ceiling with the action-space diagnostic reported beside it. Applied to our own eight submissions (\S\ref{sec:release}): every $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{diff}}$ against the paraphrase floor is negative (Table~\ref{tab:floors}), the wrong sign regardless of which value the bar takes, so criterion (i) alone rejects all eight, independent of (ii). \texttt{ECoT-bridge} clearing its $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ ceiling at $2.5\times$ therefore does not admit it: (ii) is a necessary check on the direction-aware score specifically, not a substitute for (i), and a model must pass both.

\emph{The $-0.5$ cosine threshold is not why the admission rule's clearance pattern holds.} $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$'s reversal criterion ($\cos < -0.5$, Eq.~\ref{eq:fdir}) is one choice among a range of comparably strict ones. Recomputing $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ and each configuration's own null ceiling from the same released per-sample action vectors at $\cos < -0.25$ and $\cos < -0.75$ (\texttt{scripts/\allowbreak{}fdir\_threshold\_sweep.py}) leaves the qualitative pattern unchanged at the tighter end: the same seven CoT-trained LoRA/data variants plus \texttt{ECoT-bridge} clear their own null ceiling at both $-0.25$ and $-0.5$ ($7$/$11$ each), and all three DeepThinkVLA checkpoints clear at neither (Table~\ref{tab:threshold_sweep}). At the loosest threshold tested, $-0.75$, the count rises to $8$/$11$, but not because the pattern strengthens: \texttt{no-CoT}, a null control, nominally clears by $0.007$ ($0.023$ against a $0.017$ ceiling), and \texttt{ECoT-bridge}'s own margin, a comfortable $0.070$ ($2.5\times$) at $-0.5$, shrinks to $0.003$ ($1.2\times$) at $-0.75$. A null control starting to clear and a genuine positive result losing its margin in the same direction are both signs that $-0.75$ is too loose a criterion to trust, not evidence that the admission rule is threshold-fragile in the range that matters; it is why the main text reports $-0.5$ rather than the loosest cosine threshold that still separates the two floors.

\emph{Direction-aware scoring, checked against the same alternative explanation the magnitude score cannot rule out.} \emph{direction\_flip} rewrites a lexical cue in a \emph{teacher-forced} gold CoT whose MOVE phrase was itself derived from the demonstration action, so a model could reverse its action by having memorized which MOVE string goes with which action bin, with no reasoning mediating the edit at all: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ as reported everywhere else in this paper cannot distinguish that from a genuine response to the direction word, because every number it is given is teacher-forced. Self-generated CoT breaks that specific confound: the MOVE phrase the model free-decodes is its own text, not a demonstration-derived string, so a memorized (string, action) pair from training is far less likely to sit behind it verbatim. Recomputing $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ directly from the released per-sample action vectors of the same self-generated-CoT records used above, on \emph{direction\_flip} at $t{=}0$: \texttt{r=32} clears at $0.761$ ($n{=}71$) against $0.582$ teacher-forced, \emph{higher} rather than lower; \texttt{ECoT-bridge} stays low at $0.151$ ($n{=}53$) against $0.117$ teacher-forced; \texttt{no-CoT} stays low at $0.211$ ($n{=}38$) against $0.087$. None of the three drops when the direction word moves from a demonstration-derived string to the model's own free-decoded one, which is evidence against pure memorization as the explanation for \texttt{r=32}'s clearance, though three checkpoints is the same small cohort the paragraph above already cautions against generalizing from.

\emph{A second alternative explanation for a low $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$: the edit leaves a contradicting, unedited anchor in the same prompt, and a policy that grounds in it rather than in the MOVE sentence would be behaving correctly, not unfaithfully.} \emph{direction\_flip} rewrites only the \texttt{MOVE}/\texttt{MOVE REASONING} text; the rendered prompt's \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS} bounding boxes and \texttt{GRIPPER POSITION} are left exactly as they were. A real instance, from \texttt{judge\_edit\_families/\allowbreak{}judge\_pairs.json}: gripper at $x{=}109$, target bounding box centered at $x{=}189.5$ (clearly to the gripper's right, matching the \emph{original} ``move back and right'') while the edited MOVE now reads ``move forward and left'', contradicting the still-unedited geometry in the same prompt. A policy that reads bounding-box coordinates rather than the MOVE sentence would correctly keep moving toward the (unedited) target and score as unfaithful for the right reason. We test this directly with \emph{direction\_flip\_no\_geom}: the identical MOVE/MOVE~REASONING edit, plus blanking \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS} and \texttt{GRIPPER POSITION} so no contradicting anchor remains, on the identical samples (same applicability condition as \emph{direction\_flip}, so this is a paired comparison, not a differently-scoped family). On \texttt{ECoT-bridge} (3 seeds, $N{=}100$ each, $n{=}298$ pooled): $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} = 0.090 \pm 0.028$ against $0.117 \pm 0.032$ with the geometry present, and mean translation cosine $+0.491$ against $+0.418$: removing the contradicting anchor makes the action \emph{more} similar to the unedited one, not less, and $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ \emph{falls} rather than rises. This is the opposite of what the geometric-grounding explanation predicts: if the model were reading bbox/gripper coordinates instead of the MOVE sentence and correctly ignoring a contradicted instruction, removing that alternative signal should free it to follow the text, raising $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$. It does not. We read this as evidence against (not proof against, on one checkpoint and one architecture) the specific mechanism this confound proposes, and as a further, independent sign that ECoT-bridge's low $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ is closer to the CoT genuinely not driving the action than to an artifact of what else the model can see.

\emph{A third check on the same confound: instead of removing the contradicting anchor, mirror it to agree with the flipped direction.} If a policy reads bbox/gripper coordinates rather than the MOVE sentence, making the geometry actively agree with the new direction should make compliance easier, raising $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ toward the ceiling. \emph{direction\_flip\_geom\_consistent} applies the identical MOVE/MOVE~REASONING edit, then mirrors \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS} and \texttt{GRIPPER POSITION} coordinates about the image center along the flipped axis (or axes), so the edited geometry agrees with the new instruction rather than contradicting it (\emph{direction\_flip}) or omitting it (\emph{direction\_flip\_no\_geom} above). It applies only to left$\leftrightarrow$right and up$\leftrightarrow$down flips (a 2D mirror has no forward/back analogue), a stricter subset of \emph{direction\_flip}'s own applicability, so we compare against \emph{direction\_flip} restricted to the identical samples rather than its full pooled rate. On \texttt{ECoT-bridge} (3 seeds, $N{=}100$ each, $n{=}96$ paired): $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} = 0.083$ against $0.062$ with the geometry left contradicting on the same samples, and mean translation cosine $+0.612$ against $+0.640$: both move slightly in the direction geometric grounding predicts, but by an amount far short of the $2.5\times$ ceiling clearance this checkpoint shows on its full applicable set (\S\ref{sec:directional}), and small enough at this $n$ that we do not read it as resolving the confound the way the larger, opposite-sign movement of the no-geometry check above does. Across all three geometry conditions reported for this checkpoint (contradicting, absent, agreeing), $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ stays within $0.062$--$0.117$ and mean cosine within $+0.418$ to $+0.640$: not the large, monotonic swing geometric grounding predicts under either edit, which we continue to read as evidence against, not proof against, that mechanism.

\emph{Neither check is exhaustive.} The self-generated-CoT and geometry checks rule out two specific, concrete alternative explanations for a low $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$; they do not rule out every possible one, and we do not claim they do. Both are scoped to what they actually tested: memorization on four checkpoints in one direction, geometric grounding on one checkpoint under two opposite edits. A skeptical reader should read $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$'s absolute values with that in mind, the same way \S\ref{sec:directional} already asks for the ceiling comparison rather than the raw number.

\emph{Our one constructive result is confounded with policy competence, and separately with action-space richness.} The six configurations that clear the $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ null at $6.6$--$11.1\times$ are exactly the six whose open-loop prediction does not beat a constant (\S\ref{sec:release}), and the one strong policy clears at $2.5\times$: this design does not separate ``reverses the vector when the reasoning says to'' from ``is a weak policy''. It is a second confound as well: on those six, at most one of the three translation axes is off its zero bin on $72$--$84\%$ of scored samples (roll and pitch are frozen at one bin on most samples for six of our seven LoRA variants), so $\cos < -0.5$ often reduces to a sign test on a single active axis, clearing at $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}} \mid \text{moved} = 0.85$--$0.95$; conditioning both treatment and ceiling on the action having moved at all still leaves a $5.9$--$10.7\times$ clearance, so the null is not purely an artifact of the argmax-collision confound that sinks $\mathcal{F}$ (\S\ref{sec:collision}), but it is not on the same scale as \texttt{ECoT-bridge}'s richer action space: it moves on $288$ of $299$ samples ($96\%$), so conditioning on movement barely changes its $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ ($0.122$ vs.\ $0.117$ unconditioned) and its clearance stays close to the $2.5\times$ reported throughout \S\ref{sec:directional}. An isotropic action distribution scores $0.25$ at our $\cos < -0.5$ criterion, but that reference is the wrong one for a collapsed action space: resampling each model's own edited action against a different observation's original action (a same-model permutation null) gives a chance rate of $0.38$--$0.49$ on the six collapsed configurations, \emph{above} $0.25$, and only $0.00$--$0.05$ on \texttt{ECoT-bridge} and the DeepThinkVLA family; against that null the six configurations clear by only $1.5$--$1.8\times$, not $6.6$--$11.1\times$ (ECoT-bridge, again the exception, clears at $2.5\times$ before this stricter null is even applied). $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$'s absolute values are therefore not comparable across the cohort, and an admission rule built on it should report the action-space diagnostic beside every score. One natural alternative explanation for the six-config gap is simply that they are undertrained relative to \texttt{ECoT-bridge}. Training \texttt{r=32} on the same recipe $8\times$ longer ($120{,}000$ steps) leaves both diagnostics close to where they started: $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ on \emph{direction\_flip} moves from $0.582$ to $0.569$ against a null ceiling that itself falls ($0.073\to0.057$, both \emph{cross\_task\_swap}), so the clearance ratio rises slightly ($7.9\times\to10.0\times$) rather than falling toward \texttt{ECoT-bridge}'s $2.5\times$; and the action-space-collapse diagnostic barely moves (at most one axis off its zero bin on $76.0\%\to72.7\%$ of samples, the same $89$ distinct actions among the same $300$ observations before and after). Eight times the gradient steps on an identical recipe does not close either gap, which argues against simple undertraining as the explanation and is consistent with the collapse being a property of this recipe (or of LoRA at this rank) rather than of how long it ran.

\emph{No number here is rollout-conditioned.} The leaderboard is first-step; the paired rollout returns $0/40$ in both arms, a checkpoint-competence problem rather than a compute or suite-availability one, so an edit-induced $\Delta$SR is undefined and none is reported. Training the same recipe $8\times$ longer ($120{,}000$ steps, not $15{,}000$) does not fix it either: on the tasks a 20h re-run completed before its time budget expired, SR(\emph{cot\_clean}) is $0/10$ (Wilson $95\%$ CI $[0, 0.28]$), an upper bound still below the $\geq 0.4$ this paper's own admission rule for a rollout-level result would require -- a checkpoint-competence problem, not a training-budget one, at least within the budget we could afford. The harness itself is validated, not merely trusted, against the four public LIBERO checkpoints with a published rollout SR, reproducing $0.857$--$1.018\times$ published performance (full per-suite numbers and validation history: \texttt{DATASHEET.md}); the rollout harness, its arm-pairing diagnostics and the trajectory-level readout we substituted for SR are in the release. \emph{\texttt{ECoT-bridge} is the one checkpoint we could not even probe this way}: its released norm-stats carry only \texttt{bridge\_orig}, so any action it emits on our LIBERO suite would reach the simulator at raw $[-1,1]$ scale and score $0$ independent of any edit, a corpus mismatch rather than a competence measurement (\texttt{results\_v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_runs/\allowbreak{}rollout\_probe\_ecot\_bridge}); its own paper reports $66\pm3.8\%$ real-robot success on the Bridge~V2 tasks it was trained for \citep{ecot}, so this release neither confirms nor contests its competence at that task. \emph{Per-family $N$ varies from 58 to 100} with a visibility gate, so each model is compared only against its own floor and ceiling. \emph{The retraining bar itself is estimated from the seven \texttt{Ours} configurations only} (six with a released 13-family retrain pair) and applied to \texttt{ECoT-bridge} and the three DeepThinkVLA checkpoints without a retrain replicate for any of them, so \S\ref{sec:floors}'s claim that those four rows also clear the retraining bar rests on the assumption that retraining noise of this size transfers across base checkpoints and architectures, which nothing in the release tests directly. \emph{$\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ does not transfer to the second architecture family}: all three DeepThinkVLA checkpoints fail it. \emph{OpenVLA-OFT \citep{openvlaoft} is excluded} after failing to load at its authors' declared pins.

One LIBERO episode, three arms (no-CoT, own CoT, direction-flipped), replayed from the same init state for $400$ steps, shown at $t = 0, 80, 160, 230, 310, 390$; the MOVE phrase each arm's CoT carried that step is below its row. All three start pixel-identical at $t{=}0$. The own-CoT arm barely travels, its whole path inside a $21.8$\,cm box, while the flipped and no-CoT arms reach $139.7$\,cm and $128.8$\,cm from it.}

\emph{Figure~\ref{fig:frames} illustrates, rather than measures, why we do not report rollout-conditioned faithfulness.} One episode (\emph{libero\_90} task ``close the top drawer of the cabinet'', task~$0$/episode~$0$), the CoT regenerated \emph{every} step, all three rows pixel-identical at $t{=}0$ (max mean $|\Delta\text{pixel}| = 0.0$; four rounds of arm-pairing fixes bought this and the generator verifies it before drawing). Between-column change within an arm runs $0.04$--$7.7$ absolute pixel levels, which is what lets a reader tell a stalled policy from a repeated frame. All three arms score $0$, so no $\Delta$SR is defined and this single episode of one task licenses no ranking; it is placed here to make the scope statement above concrete, not to extend it.

\paragraph{A separate, larger rollout replay measures the question directly, rather than disclosing it as a gap: does the token-level score predict where the arm actually goes?} Since in-suite success rate is $0/20$ for every arm (\texttt{cot\_clean} never solves the task either, so a delta against it is $0$ by construction and ranks nothing), the readout is \emph{end-effector path deviation from the \texttt{cot\_clean} arm of the same scene}, defined whether or not the task is solved. All $15$ arms are replayed from one init state per scene with the CoT regenerated every step, on \texttt{r=32}, over the first $80$ of $400$ steps (the approach phase), across $2$ \emph{libero\_90} scenes, paired at step $0$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix} has the pixel-level pairing verification this replay depends on).

\emph{The finding is that the token-level ranking is reproduced in behaviour, and that what it reproduces includes the construct-validity failure.} Over the $7$ families whose edit actually landed in the rendered CoT on this scene pair (the other $6$, \emph{cross\_task\_swap} among them, are excluded as inapplicable here, not as unfavorable), ranking by mean path deviation gives \emph{direction\_flip} $49.0$\,cm, \emph{negation} $21.4$, \emph{verb\_swap} $16.0$, \emph{paraphrase\_null} $7.52$, \emph{syntactic\_scramble} $7.51$, \emph{location\_swap} $2.5$, \emph{gripper\_flip} $1.3$, against a clean-arm path length of $51.4$\,cm, so \emph{direction\_flip} ends up $89.1$\,cm away at peak -- further than the clean arm travels in total. That order is \emph{exactly} the same families' $\mathcal{F}_{\text{mag}}$ order on this checkpoint, Spearman $\rho{=}+1.000$ ($p{=}0.00045$, $20{,}000$-permutation test, $n{=}7$) -- \emph{and we quote $\rho{=}+0.964$ instead}. The perfect coefficient turns on one pair this data does not resolve: \emph{paraphrase\_null} and \emph{syntactic\_scramble} are $0.011$\,cm apart in the two-scene mean and their order \emph{flips between the scenes} ($6.0$ vs.\ $8.5$\,cm on the first, $9.0$ vs.\ $6.5$ on the second), so the number we report is what the ranking scores with that pair swapped, and a reader should carry $\rho \geq 0.96$ rather than $\rho{=}1$. The mean translation cosine tracks the same ordering at $\rho{=}-0.964$ ($p{=}0.0027$). The one-step decode score is therefore a good ordinal proxy for where the arm goes on this checkpoint and this scene pair -- the strongest positive statement about $\mathcal{F}_{\text{mag}}$ in this paper.

\emph{It does not rescue construct validity, and that half matters more.} The unresolved pair is the two meaning-preserving families, and \emph{both} outrank \emph{both} of the two semantic families tested: \emph{paraphrase\_null} and \emph{syntactic\_scramble} at $7.5$\,cm each both move the arm further than \emph{location\_swap} ($2.5$) and \emph{gripper\_flip} ($1.3$); a meaning-preserving instruction paraphrase moves this policy's end effector $5.7\times$ further than flipping which way the gripper is told to go. \S\ref{sec:floors} establishes this at the token level; here it is present in the trajectory, so it is not an artifact of scoring one decode step, and the repair cannot be a better readout of the same policy.

\emph{One scene also contains an argmax collision visible in the trajectory rather than in a decode statistic.} On it, \emph{negation} and \emph{verb\_swap} produce \textbf{bit-identical rollouts} -- the same action at all $80$ steps and the same end-effector pose at all $80$ -- while their edited reasoning differs at \emph{every} step (``do not move right and down'' against ``hold right and down''), and both differ from the clean arm's action at all $80$ steps. On the other scene the same two arms agree on only $1$ of $80$ steps, so this is a property of the scene, not of the pair. \S\ref{sec:collision} decomposes this phenomenon at the token level; this is the same phenomenon over a trajectory, and we treat the exact ties this readout produces as coincidences to disclose, not agreements to score.

\emph{What this cannot support, at the same volume.} Two scenes only: a $7$-family rank correlation on this little data has an interval wide enough that only a very large $\rho$ is distinguishable from chance, which is why the permutation $p$ is reported rather than the point estimate alone, and the \emph{magnitudes} do not transfer even where the ranking does (\emph{verb\_swap} reads $8.8$\,cm on the first scene and $23.2$ on the second, a $2.6\times$ spread). Deviation is dissociation, not error: the clean arm does not solve the task either, so no arm here is closer to correct for deviating less; the \texttt{no-CoT} arm deviates $24.0$\,cm, second only to \emph{direction\_flip}. And this is $80$ of $400$ steps, the approach phase only. We therefore report this as two scenes' direction of evidence, not as a validated proxy, and no leaderboard number is restated in behavioural terms anywhere in this paper. \texttt{results\_v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_runs/\allowbreak{}rollout\_deltapath/\allowbreak{}deltapath\_report.json} carries the full per-family table, the per-scene breakdown and the excluded-family list.
